title: Dictionaries
description: Store pairs of keys and values so you can look a value up by name instead of by position.

content.text: Nobody remembers that their friend is number 14 in a list. You look them up by **name**. A dictionary links a **key** (like a name) to a **value** (like a phone number), so you find things by key instead of by counting.

items.title: List: find by position
items.text: Good when order matters. You must know the item's index.

items.title: Dictionary: find by key
items.text: Good for looking things up. Use the key you already know.

items: Wrap a dictionary in curly braces `{ }`.
Each pair is a key, a colon `:`, then its value.
`len()` counts the **pairs**, not the keys and values separately.

items.sub: Key already there? `=` **replaces** its value. Each key appears only once.
Key not there yet? `=` **creates** a new pair.

content.title: Square brackets do all three jobs

content.code:
hero = {"name": "Peter Parker", "power": "Spider webs"}
hero["power"] = "Shooting spider webs"
hero["city"] = "New York"
print(hero["city"])

steps.note: Make a dictionary with two pairs: `name` and `power`.
The key `power` already exists, so its value is **replaced**. Still two pairs.
The key `city` is new, so a third pair is **added**.
Look up the key `city` and print its value.

content.title: Watch the dictionary change
content.outro: Same `=` sign, two different jobs: replace if the key exists, add if it does not.

content.value: When the Key Is Not There

items.title: Square brackets
items.text: No blank, no `None`. The program stops with a `KeyError`.

items.title: .get()
items.text: The safe version. Gives `None`, or a fallback value you choose.

content.title: Two ways to read a missing key

content.value:
hero = {"name": "Peter Parker"}

# print(hero["age"])            # KeyError, the program stops here
print(hero.get("age"))          # None, no crash
print(hero.get("age", "unknown"))   # unknown, your own fallback

items: You can also ask **before** you look: `if "age" in hero:`
It is `True` only when that key exists.
For a dictionary, `in` checks the **keys**, never the values.
content.title: Check first with in

content.caption: `"Peter Parker"` is a value, not a key, so `in` says `False`.

content.explain: The key `gold` is missing, so `.get()` hands back the fallback you gave it: `0`.

quiz.question: Which brackets make a dictionary?
quiz.explain: Dictionaries use curly brackets. Square brackets make lists, parentheses make tuples.

quiz.question: In the pair "name": "Batman", which part is the key?
quiz.explain: The part before the colon is the key you look things up with. "Batman" is the value it points to.

quiz.question: hero holds only "name". What does  print(hero["age"])  do?
options: Stops the program with a KeyError
quiz.explain: Reading a missing key is an error. hero.get("age") is the version that hands back None instead of stopping.
